title: [Spec] Add LiLiCorr: a candidate-lattice reranker for DFlash drafts
body:
## Motivation

DFlash is trained on per-position marginals rather than on the joint block distribution, so its
drafted tokens are individually plausible yet **jointly incoherent** — slot 3 may be a fine
continuation of the prompt while contradicting the token DFlash itself chose for slot 2.

**LiLiCorr** keeps the top-`k` candidates DFlash already produces at each block position and scores
_transitions_ between adjacent candidates with a small two-layer transformer, then commits a path
through the resulting lattice greedily, left to right, instead of taking the per-slot argmax. One
network pass produces every vector, the pairwise scores are a single batched matmul, and only the
greedy walk stays sequential. **Verify is untouched, so outputs remain distributionally identical to**
**the target model's** — only acceptance length and throughput change.

* Paper: LiLiCorr: Lightweight Likelihood Correlation of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding (arXiv:2608.20530)
* Blog: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/lilicorr/
* **Companion PR — training:** NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer#2342

This PR is the **serving** half. It ships no checkpoints and no training code; the companion PR
above trains the drafters and exports them in the format this loader reads.

## Performance

**How these were produced.** Six drafters for a **Qwen3-8B** target, all trained in **NVIDIA**
**ModelOpt** on one matched contract — the same corpus, schedule and block geometry for every arm, so
no row carries a training advantage. Training data is NVIDIA's Nemotron Post-Training Dataset v2
with the multilingual split excluded, generated from the target with **thinking disabled**;
**6 epochs**; block size 16 (15 drafted slots, 16 verified); DFlash decay objective at gamma 7;
**8 nodes × 8 H100, global batch size 64** (one sequence per device, no gradient accumulation).

All six were then exported and **served through the code in this PR** on a **single H100 80GB**,
`tp_size 1`, at concurrency 1, greedy `T=0`, `--attention-backend fa3`, `draft_length 15`, mean of
two replicates, with the **whole node held exclusive per benchmark** so nothing else shared it.
Speedup is output tokens/s against an autoregressive baseline measured **in the same allocation**,
because a denominator borrowed from another node carries that node's clock into every ratio.

Three of the five alternatives — `DFlash`, `DSpark`, `Domino` — already live in this repo.

Cells are `acceptance length / speedup-vs-AR`; **★ fastest, ☆ second fastest**:

| benchmark       | LiLiCorr+conv   | LiLiCorr        | DSpark        | DFlash2         | Domino        | DFlash        |
| --------------- | --------------- | --------------- | ------------- | --------------- | ------------- | ------------- |
| gsm8k           | ★ 7.715 / 5.26x | ☆ 7.557 / 5.22x | 7.375 / 4.86x | 7.252 / 5.06x   | 7.225 / 4.87x | 6.341 / 4.59x |
| math500         | ★ 9.241 / 6.54x | ☆ 9.064 / 6.52x | 9.012 / 6.15x | 8.999 / 6.49x   | 8.976 / 6.25x | 7.909 / 5.88x |
| aime25          | ★ 8.285 / 6.03x | ☆ 8.156 / 6.03x | 8.043 / 5.61x | 7.967 / 5.91x   | 8.066 / 5.77x | 7.126 / 5.44x |
| humaneval       | ★ 7.393 / 4.01x | 7.077 / 3.93x   | 7.163 / 3.72x | ☆ 7.081 / 3.95x | 6.864 / 3.73x | 6.156 / 3.68x |
| mbpp\_sanitized | ★ 5.999 / 4.18x | ☆ 5.849 / 4.13x | 5.888 / 3.95x | 5.685 / 4.05x   | 5.679 / 3.91x | 5.027 / 3.70x |
| livecodebench   | ★ 7.975 / 5.40x | ☆ 7.754 / 5.33x | 7.775 / 5.10x | 7.601 / 5.26x   | 7.553 / 5.04x | 6.808 / 4.88x |
| alpaca\_eval    | ☆ 3.697 / 2.69x | ★ 3.656 / 2.70x | 3.588 / 2.52x | 3.467 / 2.58x   | 3.627 / 2.59x | 3.222 / 2.46x |
| mtbench         | ★ 4.014 / 2.94x | ☆ 3.939 / 2.93x | 3.957 / 2.78x | 3.748 / 2.80x   | 3.948 / 2.84x | 3.478 / 2.67x |

**Against every other approach in the table, LiLiCorr with convolutions is the fastest on all eight**
**benchmarks.** Plain LiLiCorr is the fastest on seven of the eight; the exception is humaneval, a
164-prompt slice, where DFlash2 is ahead by 0.5%.

`DFlash` is the deliberately head-free control. Against it, the reranked drafter is worth
**+9.1% to +14.6% output tokens/s** — the number to read if the question is "what does this buy over
what I already run":

| benchmark                      | gsm8k      | mbpp\_sanitized | math500    | livecodebench | mtbench   | humaneval |
| ------------------------------ | ---------- | --------------- | ---------- | ------------- | --------- | --------- |
| throughput vs head-free DFlash | **+14.6%** | **+12.9%**      | **+11.1%** | **+10.5%**    | **+9.9%** | **+9.1%** |

Every head also clears that control by **+7.60% to +21.67%** on acceptance, on every arm and every
benchmark, which is the check that a head actually loaded rather than silently falling back.

**Acceptance length is bit-reproducible under greedy decoding; throughput is not.** The replicate
spread on acceptance was 0.00% on every benchmark; on throughput it is about 0.2% within one
allocation, and about 1% across allocations.

ⓘ **Reproducing these needs `--attention-backend fa3`.** Backends that publish `seq_lens_cpu` every
step pay a device-to-host sync per block, worth about 8% here. That is a property of DFlash decoding
rather than of LiLiCorr, and the new docs subsection explains which backends are affected and why.
Backends also differ in attention numerics, so acceptance measured on different backends does not
belong in one table.

## Modifications

**No new `SpeculativeAlgorithm`, no worker subclass, no registration, no CLI flag, and no new**
**entry in any choices list.** Two environment variables gate the opt-in sampled commit described
below; nothing else reads the environment. LiLiCorr rides `--speculative-algorithm DFLASH` and is
selected by the checkpoint declaring `architectures: ["LiLiCorrDraftModel"]`, exactly as
`DFlash2DraftModel` selects the candidate selector. If you go looking for the registration, that is
why there isn't one.

10 files, **+3,076 / −1**. The single deleted line is one `if` in the draft loop that gained a
branch; everything else is an addition.

**Only four files already existed — +164 / −1 between them:**

| file                                              | added        | what                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| srt/speculative/dflash\_worker\_v2.py             | **+95 / −1** | five dispatch seams: two `__init__` assignments, the fold branch in `_maybe_build_draft_sampler`, the guarded anchor publication inside `_append_target_hidden_to_draft_kv_by_loc`, and a fourth arm on the existing three-way draft-loop branch |
| srt/models/dflash.py                              | **+2**       | `DFlashDraftModel` declares `lilicorr: Optional[nn.Module] = None` beside the existing `candidate_selector`, and stores the `rms_norm_eps` it already computes                                                     |
| docs/.../speculative\_decoding.mdx                | +34          | two subsections under "DFlash Decoding"                                                                                                                                                                           |
| test/registered/unit/spec/test\_dflash\_logits.py | +33          | one worker-stub test: the sampled arm's device gate                                                                                                                                                               |

For scale, `selector` (DFlash2 — the closest precedent, also a head on the same draft model, also
checkpoint-selected) appears on 43 lines of that worker; `lilicorr` appears on 30.

**New, self-contained:**

* `srt/models/lilicorr.py` (632) — the head, `LiLiCorrDraftModel(DFlashDraftModel)`, `EntryClass`, and the two weight-coverage checks
* `kernels/ops/speculative/lilicorr.py` (520) — three Triton kernels; see "Why the custom kernels" below
* `srt/speculative/lilicorr_utils.py` (656) — head geometry, the candidate lattice, the eager draft seam and the CUDA-graph-folded draft sampler, in one module beside `dflash_utils.py`
* `test/registered/unit/spec/test_lilicorr.py` (805) — 46 CPU tests
* `test/registered/kernels/ops/speculative/test_lilicorr_cuda.py` (216) — 18 GPU tests pinning the Triton kernels against their torch references
* `test/registered/e2e/speculative/test_dflash_lilicorr.py` (84) — the E2E server test, registered `disabled=` until a drafter is published

## The head runs inside the draft CUDA graph, and that is the whole optimization

The head is a long tail of small kernels, so what it costs is **host dispatch**, not FLOPs. It
therefore rides the seam DFlash already has for exactly this: `_maybe_build_draft_sampler` runs
before `init_cuda_graphs`, and the sampler is registered on
`draft_model_runner.capture_tail_hooks` through `make_draft_sampler_capture_hook` — the same
mechanism DFlash2's `_SelectorDraftSampler` and DSpark's `DsparkDraftSampler` use, and
`LiLiCorrDraftSampler` has the same shape as the latter: static buffers sized from the capture
buckets, host-side staging of the per-row sampling params before the replay, an in-graph philox
draw, and the drafted tokens written into a static `out` the worker reads after the replay.

Nothing in the head is capture-hostile: static shapes, no collectives at `tp=1`, no host syncs, a
fixed decode trip count, and every parameter-derived buffer built by
`materialize_inference_buffers` before capture.

**There is no `torch.compile` anywhere in this PR.** An earlier revision compiled the captured
body, on the theory that the graph removes the launches' host cost while leaving their number and
memory traffic alone. Measured end to end on one H100 — Qwen3-8B, gsm8k, greedy, `fa3`, `tp_size 1`,
both arms as sequential cells in **one allocation** so the node term cancels — it is a null:

| requests | concurrency | compiled | no compile | Δ acceptance | Δ output tok/s |
| -------: | ----------: | -------- | ---------- | -----------: | -------------: |
| 1319     | 1           | 6.9951 / 731.5 | 6.9947 / 735.6 | −0.005% | +0.56% |
| 1319     | 1           | 6.9951 / 739.7 | 6.9947 / 735.0 | −0.005% | −0.62% |
| 1319     | 32          | 7.0085 / 10179.5 | 7.0022 / 10131.9 | −0.090% | −0.47% |
| 320      | 32          | 7.0650 / 9410.8 | 7.0576 / 9489.0 | −0.105% | +0.83% |

Four pairs straddling zero, against a 1.12% spread for the *same* arm measured in two different
allocations. The fold, by contrast, is load-bearing: in the same allocation and on the same tree,
forcing the head out of the graph with `SGLANG_DFLASH_EAGER_DRAFT_SAMPLER=1` costs **−8.4%**.

So there is no dynamo surface here at all — no compile prewarm, no recompile-limit handling, no
`torch._inductor.config` mutation. The one operational note that remains is that the head should run
on the folded path: an eager fallback exists for the steps the graph cannot serve and is correct but
costs a large fraction of throughput, and because acceptance is identical either way that shows up
only in tokens/s. `build_lilicorr_draft_sampler` warns with a reason when it declines to fold, and
the worker warns once if a decode step lands on the eager head.

Two capture gaps remain, both shared with the existing DFlash heads. Prefill and extend run eager —
the eager seam is the third arm of the same `elif` chain that already carries the selector's and
plain DFlash's. And `tp>1` declines to fold, because the candidate top-k needs a packed all-gather
inside the graph.

## Convolutional drafters are supported, and the support is a refusal

The leading column of the table above is LiLiCorr composed with the grouped dynamic convolutions
that wrap each DFlash sublayer. It serves through this PR, and that is worth stating precisely,
because it is **not** a feature this PR adds.

The convolution belongs to the **DFlash backbone**, not to the reranker: `LiLiCorrDraftModel`
extends `DFlashDraftModel` and therefore inherits the `__init__` that builds it from
`conv_kernel_size` and `conv_group_size` in `dflash_config`. Both the plain and the convolutional
drafter already load and run through the same path, with no new flag and no new code.

What this PR contributes is the **refusal**. Both geometry keys default to `0`, so a checkpoint whose
config lost them builds no convolution modules at all — and the backbone loader then drops every
convolution tensor it cannot resolve. That is correct behaviour for rotary caches and the worst
possible behaviour here: all 20 tensors of a five-layer drafter disappear in silence, the draft
serves as its convolution-free parent, and the only symptom is an acceptance length that is lower
than it should be and entirely believable. `check_conv_weight_coverage` refuses any checkpoint whose
convolution tensors and built modules disagree, in either direction. Five of the CPU tests cover it:
the matched case, the convolution-free case, both silent-drop directions, and a partial checkpoint.

## Sampling the committed path (opt-in)

At `T > 0` the target samples, but the head committed the per-slot argmax and verify was handed a
point mass, so each slot was paid `p(argmax)` rather than the overlap of the two distributions.
`LILICORR_SAMPLING=1` draws each slot from `softmax(scores / T)` over that slot's candidates, at the
request's own temperature, and publishes the proposal it drew from into the same buffers the DFlash2
selector already fills — so the accept path is untouched and verify stays exact. Greedy requests
sharing the batch take the argmax and report a one-hot proposal. On Qwen3-8B it is worth about 6%
acceptance and 6% end-to-end at `T = 1`, at under 1% of the per-block wall.

Off by default, and with it unset the captured body is `select` itself rather than something
equivalent to it, so `T = 0` output is unchanged bit for bit.
`SGLANG_LILICORR_REQUIRE_SAMPLING=1` refuses to start if the mode was asked for but is not enabled.
Both are read once at import: the sampler is replayed from a captured draft graph, so a per-call
read would be a host-side branch inside a replay — happy to move them to `ServerArgs` fields
resolved at init if you would rather.

The sampled commit is additionally gated on the same supported-device condition as the selector's,
on both the folded and the eager path, because it publishes into an accept kernel that does not run
everywhere. Where it is unsupported the arm falls back to the argmax commit and the existing verify.

## Why the custom kernels

`kernels/ops/speculative/lilicorr.py` is the single largest new file after the head itself, so it is
worth saying up front what it buys. All three kernels dispatch to a value-identical torch
implementation off CUDA, which is also what makes the head exercisable in a CPU unit test.

**`lilicorr_topk_lse` — exact per-row top-k _and_ the full-vocab log-partition from one pass over**
**`[n, V]`.** The head scores log-probs normalized over the whole vocabulary, so it needs the partition
as well as the top-k. Composing that from existing ops (`torch.topk` followed by a `logsumexp`
epilogue) **reads the vocabulary logits three times and materializes two more `[n, V]` temporaries**,
and at a 150k vocabulary that read is the single largest cost in the block. Fusing them makes it one
read and no temporaries. The tile pre-selection is **exact, not approximate** — the argument is in the
function docstring and worth reading before trusting the kernel: if a top-k element's tile were not
among the k tiles with the largest maxima, k other tiles would each hold an element at least as
large, contradicting its rank.

**`lilicorr_greedy_path` — the whole left-to-right commit in one kernel.** The torch form issues
roughly three kernels per slot over `[bs, k]` tensors, so at 15 slots the decode is dozens of
few-microsecond launches and is pure launch overhead rather than arithmetic. Same recurrence, and
`tl.argmax` breaks ties toward the lower index as `Tensor.argmax` does, so the committed path is
identical.

**`lilicorr_sample_path` — that same walk with a sampled commit**, emitting the per-slot proposal the
verify needs to accept it by rejection sampling. A row with `greedy_mask` set takes `tl.argmax` on
the same fp32 node values as the greedy kernel, so one captured graph serves greedy and sampling
batches and the greedy rows walk a bit-identical path.

## Correctness

Verify is unmodified, so **this change cannot alter the distribution of emitted tokens.** Every
drafted token is still checked against the target model exactly as before; a worse drafter would show
up as lower acceptance, never as different output. That is the primary correctness argument, and it
is why the section above measures acceptance rather than task scores.

**Unit tests:** **46 CPU tests** (`test_lilicorr.py`), one worker-stub test in
`test_dflash_logits.py`, and **18 GPU tests** (`test_lilicorr_cuda.py`) pinning all three Triton
kernels against their torch reference implementations on device — vocabulary sizes straddling the
kernel's tile boundary in both directions, bf16 logits as production uses, the narrow-vocabulary
fallback, and the greedy commit at k = 1…16 including tie-breaking. Verified on an H100: 75/75 pass
across the three files. The registry validates — `validate_all_suites()` is clean over 2,487
registered tests — and every pinned pre-commit hook passes over the PR range.

**E2E:** `test/registered/e2e/speculative/test_dflash_lilicorr.py` serves the head through
`--speculative-algorithm DFLASH` with only the draft path changed, and asserts GSM8K accuracy plus
two acceptance floors. It is registered `disabled=` because no drafter is published yet, but it has
been run against one on an H100: `1 passed in 177.19s`, GSM8K 0.950, accept length 5.0392 against a
head-free DFLASH control reading 4.1694 on the same eval.

## Checklist

* Format your code according to Format code with pre-commit — every pinned hook passes over the PR range
* Add unit tests according to Run and add unit tests — 46 CPU tests (`register_cpu_ci`), 18 GPU kernel-parity tests (`register_cuda_ci`), and an E2E server test on the DFlash fixture (`register_cuda_ci`, `disabled=` pending a published drafter)
* Update documentation according to Write documentations — a subsection under "DFlash Decoding"
* Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results — see **Performance**
* Follow the SGLang code style guidance

## Design notes

The choices most likely to prompt a question, each also commented at the site.

1. **The head geometry is parsed in `srt/speculative/lilicorr_utils.py`, not as a field on
`DFlashDraftConfig`.** The shared DFLASH config therefore carries no knowledge of this head, at the
cost of one extra `dflash_config` read at model build, and `dflash_utils.py` stays at **zero**
changes.
2. **The lattice attention bias is materialized `[batch*heads, S, S]` rather than broadcast.** The
broadcast form is mathematically identical and saves a copy, but a stride-0 mask measured
**−1.75pp**. Please measure before changing it back.
3. **`F.rms_norm` rather than `sglang.srt.layers.layernorm.RMSNorm`, and a hand-rolled attention**
**module carrying `nn.MultiheadAttention`'s parameter layout.** Same math and the same state\_dict
keys in both cases. The custom-op norm is not capturable here, and the module's Python control flow
and `need_weights` bookkeeping are what make it uncapturable.
4. **The weight loader raises in both directions** — missing head tensors _and_ surplus ones — and
`candidate_topk` must be a power of two, refused at config parse. The surplus direction is live,
not hypothetical: one projection is an `Identity` when the head is as wide as the draft, so a
config omitting the head width would otherwise silently drop it and serve a different architecture
than the one trained. The power-of-two constraint comes from the tiled top-k holding its selected
tiles in a single Triton lane group; supporting other widths would mean serving the head on the
slow reference path, so it is refused at load instead of silently deoptimized.
5. **The convolution coverage check is separate from the head coverage check**, because the two look
at different namespaces: the convolution tensors are backbone parameters named
`layers.*.{attention,mlp}_conv.*`, none of which is under `lilicorr.`, so the head check cannot
see them. See "Convolutional drafters" above for why a missing check is dangerous rather than
merely untidy.
6. **The anchor is worker-owned rather than carried on `DFlashDraftInputV2`.** Carrying it there so
that filter and merge keep it aligned with the batch is the tidier design, but it measured
**−4.67% acceptance** at concurrency 32, and the drift it prevents is not detectable: reordering
cannot happen at concurrency 1 and happens constantly at 32, where acceptance reads 7.5573 and
7.5669. The measurement is recorded at the site in `set_anchor`.

## Known gaps

* **Checkpoints are not yet published.** The docs example carries a placeholder path. The companion
ModelOpt PR linked at the top adds the training and checkpoint export, including the optional
convolutions.
* **`tp>1` serves the head eagerly.** Folding it needs the candidate top-k's packed all-gather
inside the draft graph.

title: [AMD][DI][CI] Escape backticks in the SPUR drive_batch.sh heredoc
body:
## What
Escape two backticks in a comment inside the heredoc that `launch_mi355x.sh` uses to generate `drive_batch.sh` on the SPUR cluster.

## Why
The heredoc is unquoted (`<<EOF`), because it needs `$WORKDIR` and the other launch variables expanded. As a side effect, the backticked `` `| tee` `` and `` `tail -F` `` in the comment ran as command substitutions while the file was being written. Every SPUR leg logs this, for example in [run 36225745974](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36225745974) and [run 36302133557](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/36302133557):

```
launch_mi355x.sh: command substitution: line 1532: syntax error near unexpected token `|'
tail: cannot follow '-' by name
```

The legs still pass because both substitutions fail immediately and expand to nothing. But the generated comment loses those words, the errors look like a real launch failure when someone is triaging a red leg, and a bare `tail -F` reads stdin, so it could block if stdin were ever a pipe. The fix escapes them as `` \` ``, the same way the heredoc already escapes `\$`.

## Test plan
- Rendered the heredoc from the old and new versions of the script with bash. The old version reproduces both errors above. The new version produces no stderr, and the only difference in the generated `drive_batch.sh` is the restored comment text. `bash -n` passes on the launcher and on the generated script.
- Checked every unquoted heredoc under `scripts/`. These two lines were the only unescaped backticks.
- Not yet run in a nightly. The change affects only comment text in the generated file.

title: [Router] Gate readiness on peer bootstrap, and make it observable (13/13)
body:
**Stack 13 of 13.** Base: `router-peer-bootstrap-12-k8s-e2e`. 8 files changed, 716 insertions(+), 31 deletions(-)

### The stack

| # | PR | lines | what it adds |
|--:|---|--:|---|
| 1 | #40687 | 962 | the sharded tree gains `export_snapshot` / `restore_snapshot`; nothing calls them yet |
| 2 | #40688 | 2213 | `GET /internal/kv_snapshot` — the producer half; nothing consumes it yet |
| 3 | #40689 | 536 | `--kv-peer-selector`, the peer registry, the `_peers` gauges; no behaviour change |
| 4 | #40690 | 1150 | the EndpointSlice watch that fills the registry; still no consumer |
| 5 | #40691 | 1177 | `BootstrapTracker` + the fetch client; the consumer's state and transport |
| 6 | #40692 | 933 | `VettedSnapshot::from_wire` — the only bridge from wire bytes to the tree |
| 7 | #40693 | 2193 | the pump holds a `Pending` rank's batches and grafts a snapshot handed to it |
| 8 | #40694 | 1789 | the sweep: ask siblings, vet, deliver — one sweep per discovered worker |
| 9 | #40695 | 935 | fold a discovery burst into one fleet-wide fetch, plus the gap retry it enables |
| 10 | #40696 | 806 | a graft nothing witnessed asks the fleet instead of guessing |
| 11 | #40697 | 645 | component test over the real transport: same `match_prefix` answers as the source |
| 12 | #40698 | 940 | kind-cluster proof, the KV-publishing fake worker, and the RBAC/downward-API manifest |
| 13 | #40699 | 747 | `/readyz` holds until bootstrap settles; `--kv-bootstrap-seed-required`; the metrics **← this PR** |

Each PR's base is the branch below it, so every diff shown here is that
PR's own change. Review bottom-up; GitHub retargets each child to `main` as
its parent merges.

<details>
<summary>What the series does</summary>

A router replica subscribes to each worker's KV topic **mid-stream**, so every
block already resident in the engine's radix cache is invisible to it — and
engines publish `BlockStored` only as they *insert*, so a prefix cached hours
ago is never re-announced. A cache-blind replica then scatters the prefixes the
warm replicas were keeping consolidated, degrading the **engines'** locality for
the whole fleet; a rolling update does that to every replica in turn. This
series makes a booting replica pull a tree snapshot from a warm sibling over
HTTP and graft it beneath its live delta stream. Off unless `--kv-peer-selector`
is set.

Supersedes #39750, which carried the same work as one branch on a stale base.

</details>

## What this change does

A replica that boots with an empty KV tree does not just route cache-blind
itself — its dispatches scatter the prefixes the warm replicas were keeping
consolidated, so it degrades the engines' locality for the whole fleet. A
rolling update does that to every replica in turn, and with nothing in the
metrics to attribute the hit-rate drop to.

`/readyz` grows two conditions. The third holds 503 until peer bootstrap has
settled: a snapshot grafted, or every sibling having proved it has nothing, or
`--kv-bootstrap-timeout-ms` giving up. It latches, so a later scale-up can
never drag an already-serving replica back out of the Service. It is inert
unless both cache-aware routing and a peer selector are configured, so nothing
changes for a fleet that has not opted in.

The fourth is `--kv-bootstrap-seed-required`, off by default, and it exists
because condition 3 settles either way once the deadline expires — that escape
is load-bearing, and it is also why `settled()` cannot tell "seeded" from "gave
up". This one can: it holds readiness when a sweep proved siblings were there
and their tree could not be pulled. A NotReady pod stays out of the Service, so
a failed seed DELAYS that replica's readiness — and with it the rolling update,
the previous generation still serving — by up to
max(3× `--kv-bootstrap-timeout-ms`, 60s) — 30 minutes at the default — after
which the replica goes ready
and serves cache-blind. Nothing re-sweeps the failed ranks while the gate holds
(only a sweep started by a newly discovered worker can clear it), so the flag
buys a bounded delay and a louder signal, not a guarantee: on its own it does
not stall a rollout indefinitely, and a rollout whose seeds keep failing still
completes, with cache-blind replicas.

Which verdict may gate is the entire safety argument. `NoPeers` (first deploy,
single replica) and `FleetCold` (every sibling PROVED it holds nothing) are
legitimate nothing-to-inherit outcomes; gating on either bricks a boot that has
nothing to inherit — and because an unready replica leaves its own
EndpointSlice, every sibling would then see an empty peer set: a fleet-wide
deadlock with no automatic exit. Only `TimedOut` over a non-empty candidate set
counts. Two further rails cover the case the verdict genuinely cannot
distinguish, a simultaneous fleet-wide restart where every peer is booting: the
hold is bounded at max(3× the bootstrap budget, 60s), measured from first
registration, and then opens with a WARN; and it latches open the first time
`/readyz` answers 200. It cannot latch open early: while ranks are registered
and the boot sweep has not reported, the gate stays closed, because every rank
can go terminal (overflow, publisher reset, the deadline) before that verdict
arrives and a 200 in that window would latch it unchecked. The latch holds in
the other direction too — a pool can go ready on a worker that publishes no KV
events, and the first KV rank registering afterwards does not un-ready the
serving replica.

The tests assert over the verdict class rather than by example, because the
wrong answer in either direction is silent — gate too little and a bad rollout
ships, gate too much and the fleet deadlocks.

The metrics make the whole path attributable. `bootstrap_state` per rank, so a
rank stuck pending (holding its events back, heading for overflow) is visible;
`peer_snapshot_total` by fetch outcome, where a fleet pinned at `unreachable`
with a warm tree means the per-fetch bound is too small for the body rather
than a network fault; `bootstrap_rank_total` once per rank at its final
verdict; `bootstrap_sweep_total` per sweep, which is what separates a healthy
early settle on a cold fleet from burning the whole deadline — the rank
outcomes fold both into `abandoned`. Each counter family emits a zero row for
every label in its closed set, so `increase()` has a baseline for a series that
moves once per boot. `seed_failed` is emitted whether or not
the gate is armed: with it off, that gauge is the only thing that says the seed
did not land.

## Tests

`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and the lib +
component + proxy suites all pass on this branch **on its own**, not only on the
tip of the stack.

### Review pass

Reviewed with `/code-review --fix` and `/simplify`; fixes were folded into this PR's own commit and the stack was re-verified tier by tier (`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, lib + component + proxy tests on every branch).

- Fixed: the seed gate can no longer latch open before the boot sweep reports, and a first KV registration no longer un-readies a replica that is already serving.
- Bootstrap budgets raised: the whole sync defaults to 10 minutes and each step (per-fetch cap/floor, connect/read timeouts, per-peer retry backoff) is sized for it.
- File layout: this PR's code lives in `server/routes/health.rs` and `server/routes/metrics.rs`, plus `state/kv_events/bootstrap/tracker.rs` and `bootstrap.rs`; no file the stack creates exceeds ~1,300 lines.

<summary>What the series does</summary>

A kind-cluster proof of the two questions the feature exists to answer: a
replica joining a warm fleet ends up with the same cache-aware view as the
replicas it bootstrapped from, and it keeps up with new engine events afterwards
— the snapshot is spliced UNDER the live stream, not substituted for it. Plus
the rolling-update hazard: new replicas must not bootstrap from each other and
inherit an empty tree.

Ships the KV-publishing fake worker the test drives, and the manifest that wires
`POD_NAME`/`POD_NAMESPACE`/`POD_IP` from the downward API and the EndpointSlice
RBAC the peer watch needs — deferred from the discovery commit to here, where
there is something for it to exercise. The fake worker declares mirrors of the
engine's `EventBatch` / `BlockStored` structs with the same msgspec options, so
msgspec itself produces the engine's wire encoding — each event a tagged MAP
keyed by `type` — rather than a hand-built shape; the router rejects the older

but a decode failure.

events are driven by a POST rather than a timer, so nothing is ever in flight
the test did not ask for; views are compared only after every replica's cursor
has provably caught up to the worker's `last_seq`, never on a fixed sleep; and
nothing asserts on a transient mid-rollout state — the scale-up case is asserted
directly and the rollout case only after `rollout status` completes. Views are
compared canonically, since snapshot node order follows per-shard hash-map
iteration.

warm replicas were keeping consolidated, degrading the **engines'** locality for
the whole fleet; a rolling update does that to every replica in turn. This
series makes a booting replica pull a tree snapshot from a warm sibling over

is set.

## What this change does

A graft whose held queue was empty leaves its watermark unchecked until a live
batch arrives, and nothing guarantees one ever does. An idle rank would serve
grafted state forever with its continuity unproven, and a `BlockRemoved` lost in
the subscribe window would survive as a permanent false cache hit that no later
event corrects.

Silence is not evidence, so the bounded wait ends in a QUESTION, not a verdict.
Reaching the deferred path means nothing arrived between subscribing and
grafting, and the subscriber is live before the fetch — so silence is far more
often "this rank published nothing" than "we lost a delta". Discarding on a timer
would cost every quiet fleet its warm tree, which is the regression this feature
exists to prevent.

So the pump asks the fleet whether the publisher moved past the watermark. Any
peer's cursor is admissible: sequence numbers are the publisher's, so a peer
reporting one above ours proves a batch was emitted that we never saw. A peer too
cold to bootstrap from is still a valid witness, which is why the probe reads the
wire cursor directly instead of vetting. It asks for the cursor table alone, not
a snapshot — the question is answered completely by one integer per rank, and
fetching a tree to read it made the proof cost scale with the tree, so a fleet
large enough to need bootstrap was also the fleet that could not afford to prove
it.

A peer counts as a witness for a rank only when its table names that rank AT OR
ABOVE the watermark: a peer that never saw the rank, or whose cursor is below
the watermark (a stalled subscription, a reset we missed), cannot say what came
after, and counting it would manufacture a "no advance" out of ignorance. A
peer whose table carries a `SNAPSHOT_FORMAT` this build does not recognise is
skipped, the same rule vetting applies. A witness ABOVE the watermark resolves
the rank as `Advanced`, which goes through the same `resolve_gap` as the
first-batch check — discard the graft, and one retry if the tracker allows it.
A graft no batch and no peer can speak to is KEPT, tallied `warm_unwitnessed`
rather than `warm`, after `MAX_UNKNOWN_PROBES` unanswerable rounds — without a
stop, a single-replica deployment would re-probe forever and its verdict would
never resolve in the metrics.

The probe runs off-pump because it does network I/O; the verdicts come back over
the pump's own control channel so the tree write stays on the single writer. It
runs as ONE pass per sweep tick for every due rank, fetching each peer's cursor
table at most once and judging every rank against it, so idle ranks do not
multiply the fleet's work. A pass is capped by `SPLICE_PROBE_BUDGET`, one tick
short of the proof timeout, so passes never overlap and a hung peer cannot
stack up concurrent passes; a peer not reached inside the budget is simply not
a witness this pass. Each verdict carries the graft's watermark as well as its
epoch: a gap retry re-grafts under the same incarnation, so a stale verdict
about the previous graft is recognised and ignored. A verdict that never lands
(a panicked probe task, say) does not freeze the rank: it is re-probed once
the timeout since the last launch elapses.

## What this change does

A peer snapshot is fleet-wide: one body carries the whole worker table, every
cursor, and the whole tree, so a single fetch already contains everything every
pending rank needs. `add_worker` fires once per discovered engine, so sweeping
from there re-downloads that same document once per engine — and the document
grows with the fleet while the fetch count grows with it too. On a 168-engine
fleet that is 168 fetches of a multi-megabyte body per booting replica, most of
which time out and leave their ranks cold.

`add_worker` now hands its obligations to a coordinator that serialises
bootstrap into one sweep at a time and lets every rank pending when that sweep
lands share its snapshot. The fetch is not delayed to collect a batch first
because it does not need to be: the sweep IS the collection window — a
multi-megabyte transfer takes far longer than an EndpointSlice watch event
takes to deliver a fleet, so ranks discovered while it is in flight merge into
the same delivery at no latency cost.

Sharing is safe because the invariant is a SEQUENCE condition, not a wall-clock
one. Vetting runs against the live-worker set at the moment the body arrives, so
a worker discovered during the fetch is already covered; and the watermark check
adjudicates every rank independently, so a rank whose publisher did advance in
between is discarded to `Gap` rather than spliced over a hole.

Sharing one snapshot only helps if it is fresh enough for every rank sharing it,
and ranks in a batch begin holding at different moments — so the sweep asks with
the strictest floor among them. That guarantee covers the ranks it STARTED with;
a batch merged in afterwards was not represented in the request. Discovery
accepts that trade, a gap retry does not, which is what `LateJoin` distinguishes.

That retry is the other half of this change. A gap is the costliest failure —
a snapshot fetched, grafted, then thrown away because the live stream did not
join its watermark — and a fresher snapshot usually splices. It needs somewhere
to put the rank back, which is the queue this change introduces, so until now a
gapped rank was terminal. The tracker caps it at one retry per rank, and the
retry is stamped NOW and refuses to ride an in-flight sweep, or it would be
adjudicated against a snapshot taken before the gap and re-gap by construction.

retry starts from exactly the shape a first attempt does — no tree state, no
cursor, every delta held — and nothing is applied under the retry's graft to
be filtered later against its seeded cursor. `Gap` is tallied only as a final
verdict; a granted retry records nothing, and the retry's own resolution
records the rank's one `RankOutcome`.

## What this change does

The producer half now has a consumer. A booting replica asks its siblings for a
cache-aware tree, vets what comes back, and hands it to the pump — which has
been able to graft one since the previous change but had nothing to graft.

The sweep retries rather than asking once. Worker discovery regularly completes
before the peer watch has delivered its first EndpointSlice list, so a single
pass sees zero candidates and abandons, and the joining replica boots cold
beside warm siblings. The bootstrap deadline bounds the whole search, not each
request, so a fleet of slow peers cannot outlast the readiness gate.

The per-fetch timeout is a strict fraction of that deadline, not the deadline
itself. `reqwest`'s total timeout would otherwise let the first unresponsive
peer starve every other candidate — the outer deadline then cancels the sweep
mid-fetch and the replica boots cold having tallied no peer outcome at all.
`--kv-bootstrap-fetch-timeout-cap-ms` bounds the derivation from above, so a
deliberately generous readiness budget still cannot park on one hung peer; the
router warns at startup when the derived value lands below the floor a
multi-megabyte body needs, because that failure otherwise looks like every peer
being unreachable with the configured cap looking blameless.

Accepting a snapshot is not the same as accepting a peer. A body can vet
cleanly and still know nothing about the ranks being bootstrapped, so the sweep
keeps looking rather than ending on it; a peer whose snapshot is permanently
incompatible is never re-fetched; and one that simply has nothing right now
sits out a few passes, doubling on each repeat miss up to about 30s, because
retrying every 250ms means re-downloading a multi-megabyte tree from a replica
that is itself serving traffic.

`PumpControl`, which is what releases the ranks from `Pending`. The cold-fleet
verdict is discarded if the candidate set changed mid-pass: a peer that was
never consulted holds state that, unlike post-subscription events, cannot be
recovered later.

A sweep runs only for ranks newly registered with the tracker: `register`
returns obligations for newly inserted ranks alone, decided under its lock, so
re-adding a worker the tracker already holds — as
`reconcile_unresolved_workers` does — starts no second sweep. A `Pending` rank
already has one, and a terminal rank has nothing left to fetch; a rank
`remove_worker` forgot comes back as a new incarnation and is swept again.

fetches the same fleet-wide body once per worker; the coordinator that folds a
discovery burst into a single fetch is the next change.

consumes: the sweep that fetches one from a warm sibling lands next.

A rank registered with the tracker enters `Pending`, and the pump buffers its
KV batches instead of applying them. That hold is what makes a graft sound: a
snapshot exported at the peer's cursor C is only safe to splice under a live
stream that resumes at C+1, and a rank already applying deltas has no such
seam left to splice into.

The hold is capped per rank. Reaching the cap abandons bootstrap for that rank
(`RankOutcome::Overflow`), and the held queue — intact, since nothing was
dropped to reach the cap — is REPLAYED as live deltas rather than discarded:
discarding it would lose every block stored while waiting, blocks the engine
never re-announces. The cap counts batches, not bytes, so a held batch drops

a long-context fleet cannot hold gigabytes at boot.

tree — it hands a `VettedSnapshot` to the pump through `PumpControl`, and

all on the pump task. `PumpControl` is also how a rank leaves `Pending` when no
snapshot arrives: every exit path sends exactly one message, which is what
guarantees held batches are eventually released rather than buffered until the
per-rank cap overflows.

the rank's first live batch has arrived, so there is nothing to compare the
watermark against yet; the check runs on whichever batch turns up first, held or

stream that can never join it, not as an overflow.

per rank, not process-wide: a process-wide counter would let one worker's re-add
invalidate another worker's in-flight task. `RankOutcome` and `SnapshotOutcome`

the other counts peers that were asked — because a single peer answers for many

whose snapshot is big enough to be worth having — the failure gets MORE likely
the warmer, i.e. the more useful, the fleet's tree becomes. So `connect_timeout`
cuts a peer that is gone, `read_timeout` cuts one that stopped sending mid-body,
and the total bounds only a transfer that is progressing.

while `::` (dual-stack on Linux) and a hostname keep both. Each ready endpoint
yields its first address only, and a sibling listed once per family is offered

be thrown away. `max_age_ms` is measured from the request's ARRIVAL, not from
when it gets the cache lock: an export sampled after the caller arrived meets
any `max_age`, however long a build kept it queued. The build is
single-flighted behind an async mutex and the encoded body is cached, so a boot
herd shares one tree walk; the build runs detached and owns the lock, so a
caller that gives up mid-build does not cancel it and the result still fills
the cache. The entry is stamped BEFORE the cursors are read, so it never claims
to cover more of the publisher's stream than it does, and each cursor is
re-checked against the live map after the walk: one that went backwards or
vanished means that rank's publisher reset (or the rank was re-added) during
the walk, so it is dropped and the consumer runs that rank cold rather than
filtering the new stream against the old stream's position.

`?cursors_only=true` answers the cursor table alone, read live with no cache.
A splice probe asks one question — is your cursor for this rank above my
watermark? — and paying a full tree export for it costs a walk, a
multi-megabyte serialise and a compress, per peer per probe. That table is
deliberately a SUPERSET of the export's, which is filtered to ranks still
carrying nodes: a graft recipient needs a block source, but a witness only
needs to have seen the publisher's stream. Its `nodes` is always empty, which
makes the body ungraftable by construction rather than by discipline.

Compression is the producer's, not a middleware layer's. Each build encodes
the body once as JSON and once as gzip (`SnapshotBody { identity, gzip }`) on
the blocking pool, and both are cached, so a boot herd pays the serialise and
the compress once per build rather than once per request. The route serves the
gzip with `Content-Encoding: gzip` only when `Accept-Encoding` asks for it — a
`q=0` weight is a refusal — and the identity JSON otherwise, with
`Vary: accept-encoding`. It is the only response here big enough to be worth
compressing, so nothing is added to the proxy path. The level is
`Compression::fast()`: the body is highly repetitive, so level 1 already
shrinks it several-fold, and this runs on a replica serving traffic during a
boot herd. A body that fails to encode is never cached and answers `503`, which
a consumer reads as "no snapshot here".

## Tests

`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and the lib +
component + proxy suites all pass on this branch **on its own**, not only on the
tip of the stack.

### Review pass

Reviewed with `/code-review --fix` and `/simplify`; fixes were folded into this PR's own commit and the stack was re-verified tier by tier (`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, lib + component + proxy tests on every branch).

- Fixed: waiters now share one snapshot build, and a build whose requester gave up still fills the cache (the build runs detached and owns the lock).
- File layout: this PR's code lives in `state/kv_events/index/producer.rs` (new), `state/kv_events/bootstrap.rs` (new) and `server/routes/cache.rs`; no file the stack creates exceeds ~1,300 lines.
- Also moves the pre-existing `index::tests` module verbatim into `index/tests.rs` (the ~630-line delete/add pair), so `index.rs` stays small.

title: [Router] Give the cache-aware tree a snapshot surface (1/13)
body:
**Stack 1 of 13.** Base: `main`. 2 files changed, 945 insertions(+), 17 deletions(-)

### The stack

| # | PR | lines | what it adds |
|--:|---|--:|---|
| 1 | #40687 | 962 | the sharded tree gains `export_snapshot` / `restore_snapshot`; nothing calls them yet **← this PR** |
| 2 | #40688 | 2213 | `GET /internal/kv_snapshot` — the producer half; nothing consumes it yet |
| 3 | #40689 | 536 | `--kv-peer-selector`, the peer registry, the `_peers` gauges; no behaviour change |
| 4 | #40690 | 1150 | the EndpointSlice watch that fills the registry; still no consumer |
| 5 | #40691 | 1177 | `BootstrapTracker` + the fetch client; the consumer's state and transport |
| 6 | #40692 | 933 | `VettedSnapshot::from_wire` — the only bridge from wire bytes to the tree |
| 7 | #40693 | 2193 | the pump holds a `Pending` rank's batches and grafts a snapshot handed to it |
| 8 | #40694 | 1789 | the sweep: ask siblings, vet, deliver — one sweep per discovered worker |
| 9 | #40695 | 935 | fold a discovery burst into one fleet-wide fetch, plus the gap retry it enables |
| 10 | #40696 | 806 | a graft nothing witnessed asks the fleet instead of guessing |
| 11 | #40697 | 645 | component test over the real transport: same `match_prefix` answers as the source |
| 12 | #40698 | 940 | kind-cluster proof, the KV-publishing fake worker, and the RBAC/downward-API manifest |
| 13 | #40699 | 747 | `/readyz` holds until bootstrap settles; `--kv-bootstrap-seed-required`; the metrics |

Each PR's base is the branch below it, so every diff shown here is that
PR's own change. Review bottom-up; GitHub retargets each child to `main` as
its parent merges.

<details>
<summary>What the series does</summary>

A router replica subscribes to each worker's KV topic **mid-stream**, so every
block already resident in the engine's radix cache is invisible to it — and
engines publish `BlockStored` only as they *insert*, so a prefix cached hours
ago is never re-announced. A cache-blind replica then scatters the prefixes the
warm replicas were keeping consolidated, degrading the **engines'** locality for
the whole fleet; a rolling update does that to every replica in turn. This
series makes a booting replica pull a tree snapshot from a warm sibling over
HTTP and graft it beneath its live delta stream. Off unless `--kv-peer-selector`
is set.

Supersedes #39750, which carried the same work as one branch on a stale base.

</details>

## What this change does

A router replica subscribes to each worker's KV topic mid-stream, so every
block already resident in the engine's radix cache is invisible to it. The
recovery paths for that — pulling tree state from a warm sibling, or later
from the worker itself — all need the same thing first: a way to get the
tree out and back in without losing what it knows.

Add that surface and nothing else. `export_snapshot` emits a flat,
parent-linked node list in DFS pre-order; `restore_snapshot` grafts one back,
creating nodes that are absent and unioning carriers into nodes that are
present, so restoring onto a live tree is well defined.

Records are parent-linked by INDEX, not by block hash. The same hash
legitimately occupies several tree positions, so a hash-keyed replay would
land in `resolve_parent`'s ambiguous branch and could graft a chain under the
wrong node. Full root-to-node hash paths would be unambiguous too, and
quadratic in depth against chains that run thousands of blocks deep.

Tiers ride along per carrier, parallel to `workers` by index, and
`SnapshotNode::retain_carriers` is the only correct way to filter that pair —
filtering `workers` alone silently re-pairs every later carrier with another
carrier's tiers. An absent `tiers` list reads as device, which is what a
carrier list meant before tiering existed, so the format needs no version bump
in either direction. A tier entry naming only bits this build does not rank is
DROPPED rather than folded onto device: folding would make a future tier's
carrier a preferred device owner here, which is the trade `Tiers::for_store`
already refuses to make for an unknown `medium`.

A snapshot arrives over the network, so shape is validated before any
mutation: backward parent references, in-range worker indices, and a tier list
that either pairs one-to-one with its carriers or is absent. `restore_snapshot`
stays `pub(in crate::state::kv_events)` — the ids in a worker table must be resolved against the
live worker set, never deserialized straight off the wire.

Both passes take the shards one at a time and release a shard's lock every
4096 records. Sharding caps how much of the tree one lock covers, not how long
a pass over that much of it runs, so an unchunked walk would still stall every
match and every publisher cursor rooted in the shard being walked. The result
is a point-in-time aggregate rather than one consistent instant, which is what
a consumer grafting beneath a live delta stream already tolerates. Restore
holds the tree's writer mutex across those gaps, so the other writer cannot
prune a parent an earlier chunk placed and a later chunk hangs a child from.

A snapshot records no shard column. Restore re-derives a chain's shard from its
root hash, landing it where `insert` would have — so a chain that a racing
prune had stranded under some other shard's sentinel is rebuilt where
`match_prefix` can reach it, instead of being copied stranded onto the consumer.

## Tests

`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and the lib +
component + proxy suites all pass on this branch **on its own**, not only on the
tip of the stack.

### Review pass

Reviewed with `/code-review --fix` and `/simplify`; fixes were folded into this PR's own commit and the stack was re-verified tier by tier (`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, lib + component + proxy tests on every branch).

- Fixed: carrier-less records are no longer grafted — a record left with no carrier and no carrying descendant (e.g. after the tier filter) is skipped, so restore cannot leave an empty leaf that turns its parent's hit into a match with no workers.
- File layout: this PR's code lives in `state/kv_events/tree/snapshot.rs` (new), a child module of `tree.rs`, plus a small change to `tree.rs` itself; no file the stack creates exceeds ~1,300 lines.

title: [Benchmark] Add synthetic audio input to bench_serving
body:
## Motivation

`bench_serving` has no audio workload generator, so audio-capable models cannot be exercised through an equivalent of its synthetic image benchmark. This adds an `audio` dataset for measuring serving latency and throughput through `sglang-oai-chat`.

Related to #8072. This continues the audio benchmarking effort proposed by @Jenson97 in #27448, adapted to the current dataset and message-list interfaces. A coordination note is posted in [the issue](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/8072#issuecomment-5844045155).

## Modifications

- Generate reproducible mono PCM16 WAV clips at 16 kHz using existing NumPy and standard-library WAV encoding. Configure clip duration/count; support zero-clip controls and randomized clip counts.
- Send `input_audio` content through the existing OpenAI chat request path.
- Require server-reported `usage.prompt_tokens` for audio requests in streaming and non-streaming modes, including warmup. Missing or invalid usage fails the request instead of reporting a text-only estimate as total input.
- Report submitted audio seconds and throughput for successful measured requests, excluding warmup and failures. Leave unsupported text/vision token splits unset. Other datasets retain their existing accounting.
- Add CPU regression tests and document the command.

Initial scope is synthetic audio performance testing through `sglang-oai-chat`. Native `/generate` transport and transcription accuracy evaluation are outside this PR.

## Accuracy Tests

Rebased onto `df1fc6ab6441abbdf21944958b131c03e0921253`. On macOS arm64 with Python 3.12.9, PyTorch 2.13.0, and Transformers 5.12.1:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python python -m pytest -q \
  test/registered/unit/benchmark/test_audio_dataset.py \
  test/registered/bench_fn/test_benchmark_datasets_api.py \
  test/registered/bench_fn/test_bench_serving_reasoning_stream.py
```

**68 tests passed:** 13 new tests and 55 existing tests. The new tests exercise WAV decoding, seeded workloads, actual CLI-to-loopback-HTTP execution, both response modes, warmup failures, partial failures, and saved JSON accounting. Changed executable-line coverage is **95% (100/105)**.

Applicable pre-commit hooks and test registration validation passed on all changed files. Local documentation validation and link checks passed with Mint 4.0.1162; upstream CI uses 4.2.559.

**Real audio-model GPU validation is pending.** These CPU fixtures validate the benchmark client, not model inference or end-to-end model compatibility.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No GPU benchmark results or performance-improvement claim yet. Submitted audio duration is recorded separately from model-processed duration because audio processors may pad or truncate inputs.

## Checklist

- [x] Format changed files with the applicable pre-commit hooks.
- [x] Add registered CPU regression tests.
- [x] Update documentation.
- [ ] Complete a real audio-model smoke test and record benchmark results.
- [x] Follow SGLang code style guidance.

## Review and Merge Process

Ready for implementation review and upstream CI. Real audio-model GPU validation and required approvals remain pending.

title: [KDA+Kimi K3] Speed up SANA-Video residual gate add on H200
body:
## Motivation and changes

Speed up SANA-Video's residual-gate add on H200 using the **KDA-1.5 + Codex CLI + Kimi K3** candidate. Its transposed residual layout makes the original CUDA implementation expensive; the Triton path tiles along the physical stride-1 token dimension and preserves the original multiply-round-add semantics, output strides, guards, custom-op/fake interface and fallback.

**This PR now changes one production file and retains one kernel family: `residual_gate_add`.** The other 39 families from the earlier version have been removed entirely: any family with a measured regression, or without established material end-to-end benefit, stays at the upstream implementation. No per-shape salvage was used. Existing repository tests are unchanged, and the `kernel-design-agents` coauthor is retained.

Baseline: `c842d32b0ab45753178c5f6420662d7812766aca`. Candidate: `76aa0c6c8db3efd275a250a4b9aa07fd13b23a5a`. All results below were freshly measured with this isolated one-file candidate, so the E2E results are attributable to the retained change. The earlier 40-family combined results are not used as evidence for this revision.

## Kernel validation

NVIDIA H200; three independent processes; CUPTI cold-L2 timing. Speedup is baseline latency / candidate latency. Every original frozen case remains included; two additional actual SANA-Video layouts are reported separately. All measured ratios are at least 1; this is a statement about the tested cases, not a guarantee for arbitrary inputs.

| Workloads | Cases | Three geometric-mean speedups | Worst ratio across all repeats |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Original frozen suite | 33 | 1.2702× / 1.2686× / 1.2698× | 1.0017× |
| SANA-Video captured layouts | 2 | 2.5418× / 2.5434× / 2.5416× | 2.5385× |

SANA layout: BF16 `[1, 32760, 2240]`, transposed residual/output, contiguous update, broadcast gate with the two captured storage offsets. Latency is approximately **331 μs → 130 μs**. Captured-layout correctness and changed-input prepared calls pass. **35 existing residual-gate tests pass**, including dtype/layout/offset, compile, graph and fallback coverage.

[Raw kernel results](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/kernel-benchmarks.json) · [Existing tests](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/existing-tests.log) · [KDA provenance](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/provenance.json) · [All 40 inclusion/removal decisions](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/selection.json)

## Isolated end-to-end results

Model: `Efficient-Large-Model/SANA-Video_2B_480p_diffusers`, revision `db5f398b13ca086d09a50ce156c20527773841b1`; one H200; 832×480, 81 frames, 50 steps, guidance 6, seed 42. Prompt: `A curious raccoon walks through a sunlit forest. motion score: 30.` Eager native SGLang backend; fixed settings and pinned checkpoint in both arms.

Each quality runs two independent **A–B–B–A groups**, eight full saved requests total. Each cell compares the mean of two baseline requests with the mean of two candidate requests. Saved E2E includes scheduler wait and output saving; loading and separately captured profiling runs are excluded. Both groups must improve by at least 1.5% to qualify.

| Quality | Saved E2E group 1 | Saved E2E group 2 | Actual before/after |
|---|---|---|---|
| lossless | 38.840 → 38.190 s (**−1.67%**) | 38.810 → 38.155 s (**−1.69%**) | ![Actual before/after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/models/lossless/comparison.gif) |
| high | 36.300 → 35.670 s (**−1.74%**) | 36.295 → 35.700 s (**−1.64%**) | ![Actual before/after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/models/high/comparison.gif) |

All eight generated videos per quality are **file-byte and decoded-pixel exact**. GIF previews show baseline left and candidate right. Separate profiles confirm the changed `_rga_transposed` device branch executes in the real request.

- **lossless:** [baseline MP4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/models/lossless/baseline.mp4), [candidate MP4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BBuf/sglang/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/models/lossless/candidate.mp4), [eight-run timing](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/models/lossless/abba.json), [exact-output audit](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/models/lossless/media-audit.json), [device dispatch](https://github.com/BBuf/sglang/blob/42d1d19e5f876e7b5977fb55d90073230bce1655/diffusion-prs/kda-residual-gate-h200-20260927/models/lossless/device-dispatch.json).

title: [HiCache][perf] Queue and batch write-through backups off the request-finish path
body:
## Motivation

With `--enable-hierarchical-cache` (write_through) the unified radix cache backs up every new tree node to host. After #39050 the D2H submits are merged per step, but the per-node bookkeeping that precedes a submit still runs inside `cache_finished_req`, on the scheduler thread, at the moment the node is inserted: `build_backup_spec` (SWA/Mamba transfer lists, `torch.cat`/`clone`), host pool `alloc` for KV + side pools (with SWA host eviction when that pool is full), `resolve_host_transfers`, `commit_backup`, `inc_lock_ref`, and the ack bookkeeping. On Inkling-Small-NVFP4 that is ~0.2 ms per node, and most of it is fixed per-call torch-op and Python overhead on small tensors, not per-token work.

The workload that exposes it finishes many requests in the same scheduler step (128 lanes, four output lengths). A 64-request finish wave is tens of ms of CPU inside `process_batch_result`, longer than the ~11 ms the GPU needs for the next step, so the launch of the next batch waits and the GPU idles. At higher load (192 lanes) the scheduler is close to CPU-bound and every extra microsecond of bookkeeping shows up in throughput.

Profile on 4x GB300, Inkling-Small-NVFP4, mxfp8 KV, TP=4, 128 lanes x 16 turns, torch profiler with Python stacks over 400 steps, main at c3aa09b0db:

| 400 scheduler steps | L1 | L2 (main) |
|---|---|---|
| compute stream busy | 75.7% | 68.6% |
| GPU idle | 1,105 ms | 1,606 ms |
| radix insert wall / in GPU-idle | 213 / 185 ms | 326 / 278 ms |
| `_execute_and_commit_kv_backup` (192 nodes) | - | 106 ms, 85% in GPU-idle |
| forward launch in GPU-idle (launch waited for the CPU) | 74 ms | 261 ms |

The backup stream itself is idle almost all the time (in a 192-lane trace it overlaps 2% of the compute-stream idle time), so the cost is the scheduler-thread CPU, not the copies.

## Modifications

1. **Queue write-through backups** instead of executing them at insert time.
   - `BackupKV` actions from the insert walk go through `_queue_write_through_backup`: each node of the chain is locked (`inc_lock_ref`, the same write-through lock the immediate path takes after the backup) and appended to `queued_backups` in chain order, ancestors first. Nothing else happens on the request-finish path.
   - `flush_pending_backups()` (already called at the end of every `process_batch_result` and from `check_hicache_events`) drains up to `SGLANG_HICACHE_BACKUP_NODES_PER_STEP` nodes, oldest first.
   - `writing_check(write_back=True)` drains the queue before its blocking wait, so every queued node is acked.
2. **Batch the drained nodes.** A drain builds each node's spec in order, then backs the batch up with one host allocation per pool (KV, SWA, Mamba, sidecars) and one `CacheOperation` whose ack lists every node. The allocation is split back per node and committed node by node, exactly as the immediate path commits.
   - If a node's covered set (the node plus the SWA nodes its transfer carries) intersects the batch, i.e. an ancestor already in the batch sits in its sliding window, the batch is committed first and the node's spec is rebuilt. It then sees that ancestor backed up, as the node-by-node path would, so no SWA slot is backed up twice.
   - If the merged allocation fails, the batch falls back to the node-by-node path, which handles host eviction and failures exactly as before.
   - `HybridCacheController.write` takes an optional `node_ids` for the multi-node ack.
3. **The queue stays opt-in**: default `SGLANG_HICACHE_BACKUP_NODES_PER_STEP=0` keeps the insert-time path byte for byte (`_execute_and_commit_kv_backup` still serves it and the write-back demote path). 16 was measured on Inkling/GB300, where 8 backlogged; other values are untested. Flipping the default is left to a follow-up because the queued path differs from the insert-time path in two Mamba cases (covered by `test_mamba_path_state_cap.py`, which assumes insert-time backups):
   - The queue-time lock keeps a queued node's Mamba state safe from the per-path cap even when its first backup attempt fails. The insert-time path leaves such a node unlocked, so the cap can tombstone it before the retry.
   - A backup deferred to the flush carries a Mamba value that the same insert re-stamped. The insert-time path runs the walk backup before the commit hooks, so it excludes that value.

What changes while a node waits in the queue: it is locked, so it cannot be evicted, and it is not yet `backuped`, so a later chain that reaches it sees it queued and skips it. If a queued node is split by a later match, the new parent is not backed up until a chain passes through it; the request that caused the split holds the path lock until it finishes and inserts, which emits that chain. If that request aborts instead, the child's host copy is unreachable until host eviction reclaims it. This is a transient host-space leak, not a correctness issue.

Not changed: what is backed up (`hicache_backup_bytes_total` is identical in every arm: 91.55 GiB at 128 lanes and 137.32 GiB at 192, SWA and Mamba pools included), the ack protocol, the tree core, and the Rust core.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_unified_radix_cache_unittest.py::TestUnifiedRadixCacheQueuedWriteThrough` (8 cases):
  - queue -> flush -> ack lifecycle with lock and pending-mark checks;
  - per-step cap;
  - a queued node split before its backup;
  - host alloc failure releases the lock;
  - the default (cap 0) keeps the insert-time backup;
  - disjoint nodes share one host allocation;
  - a failed merged allocation falls back to node by node;
  - a child in the SWA window of a batched parent commits after it.
  The last three were negative-controlled: without the batching they fail, and without the overlap check the SWA case fails.
- `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/` (python core): the same failures as the base commit, none new.
- The queued, batched path issues the same transfers as the immediate one; see the backup bytes above.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

4x GB300, Inkling-Small-NVFP4, TP=4, 16 turns, `--kv-tokens 2097152 --mamba-slots 1024` (192 lanes: `3145728 / 1536`, since 2M retracts there). Throughput loss is relative to L1 (HiCache off) in the same session, with interleaved rounds (n = rounds per cell). Single-run noise is about +-0.5 pt.

Upstream main 752801e4d1 + this PR. With batching, MXFP8 lands within 0.3-0.5 pt of BF16. The only MXFP8-specific cost left on the backup path is the scale-plane submit, about 0.1% of wall time. The main column has only two rounds, so read the 192-lane MXFP8 row as no change:

| lanes | KV dtype | L2 loss, main | L2 loss, this PR with `SGLANG_HICACHE_BACKUP_NODES_PER_STEP=16` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | BF16 | 2.1% (n=2) | **0.85%** (n=5) |
| 128 | MXFP8 | 2.5% (n=2) | **1.2%** (n=5) |
| 192 | BF16 | 2.6% (n=2) | **1.9%** (n=5) |
| 192 | MXFP8 | 1.9% (n=2) | **2.4%** (n=5) |

Main 16e353d93e, MXFP8, which isolates the two parts:

| lanes | main | queue only (cap 16) | queue + batching |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 1.46% (n=2) | 1.12% (n=2) | **0.39%** (n=4) |
| 192 | 3.0% (n=4) | 3.4% (n=2) | **2.1%** (n=6) |

Why a per-step cap rather than draining the whole queue at the end of the step (same-step batching). Upstream main 752801e4d1, MXFP8, interleaved rounds in one session:

| lanes | L1 tok/s | main | same-step batching (cap = inf) | cap 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 (n=2) | 12,355 | 2.51% | 1.04% | 1.05% |
| 192 (n=5) | 14,571 | 3.06% | 2.90% | **2.26%** |

At 128 lanes batching alone is enough. At 192 lanes the request-finish waves are larger: draining a whole wave at the end of one step still lands in that step's GPU bubble, and only spreading it over the following steps recovers the throughput. A 400-step trace can miss the large waves, so this was measured end to end rather than read off a profile.

On 4x B200 (x86, slow gloo), 192 lanes, MXFP8: main 2.2% -> queue only 1.8% -> queue + batching 1.3%.

The queue alone mostly moves work around; the gain comes from batching, which turns per-node host allocs, side-pool resolves, SWA evictions and ack ops into one per batch (about 13 nodes per batch at 192 lanes). With the Rust tree core (`SGLANG_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE_CORE_BACKEND=rust`) the 192-lane MXFP8 loss drops further to 1.7% (n=2), with L1 itself 4% faster. The pre-#39050 commit ffe98a4279 measured 5.5% at 128 lanes on the same setup.

title: [HiSparse] fix: return HiSparse slots on PD decode waiting abort and DeepSeek V4 free
body:
## Motivation

Two request exits give a request's KV back without returning its HiSparse slots, and the idle leak check is skipped under HiSparse, so both leaks are silent:

1. **PD decode abort of a waiting request.** Transferred requests are admitted with `admit_request_direct` (device buffer + host slots) before they enter `waiting_queue`. Aborting one from the queue only calls `release_kv_cache`; `alloc_device_buffer` already zeroed the mapping, so nothing frees the buffer or the host pages. Every such abort leaks `padded_buffer_size` device slots plus the request's host pages, and `hisparse_req_budget` shrinks with it.
2. **DeepSeek V4 `free()`.** `DeepSeekV4HiSparseTokenToKVPoolAllocator.free()` frees only the logical pool, while the non-V4 allocator also calls `free_hisparse`. `alloc_extend` maps every compressed token to a C4 slot, so any exit that does not go through the coordinator (a request finished at prefill, an aborted chunked request) leaks its C4 pages, and `full_available_size` (bounded by the C4 pool) shrinks until admission stalls.

## Modifications

- `Scheduler.abort_request`: on a PD decode waiting-queue abort, call `hisparse_coordinator.request_finished(req)` before `release_kv_cache`, as the finish paths do.
- `DeepSeekV4HiSparseTokenToKVPoolAllocator.free`: call `free_hisparse` after the logical free, matching the non-V4 allocator. Paths that already went through the coordinator zeroed the mapping, so this frees nothing twice.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_free_returns_c4_slots` (real `DeepSeekV4TokenToKVPool` with HiSparse + real allocators): on main the C4 pool ends at `192 != 256` (one page leaked); with this change it returns to baseline and the mapping is cleared.
- Before removing the mocked waiting-abort test, `test_hisparse_allocator.py`, `test_priority_scheduling_disaggregation.py`, and `test_hisparse_unit.py`: 45 passed, 2 skipped. The suites have not been rerun after that test removal.

title: [HiSparse] fix: reject speculative decoding and mixed chunk at startup
body:
## Motivation

`validate_hisparse` accepts two combinations that crash the scheduler on the first request:

- **Speculative decoding + HiSparse.** The draft worker's `HiSparseDSATokenToKVPool` never gets a HiSparse mapping registered, so the first draft extend dies in `translate_loc_to_hisparse_device`:
  `AttributeError: 'HiSparseDSATokenToKVPool' object has no attribute 'full_to_hisparse_device_index_mapping'`.
- **`--enable-mixed-chunk` + HiSparse.** Mixing a prefill into the HiSparse decode batch fails in `merge_batch`:
  `TypeError: can only concatenate list (not "NoneType") to list`.

Both were reproduced on a 4-layer DeepSeek-V3.2 config with dummy weights (one H200, greedy, `--disable-radix-cache`). The control arms are identical to each other, so each crash is specific to the combination:

| arm | result |
|---|---|
| no spec, no HiSparse | reference |
| HiSparse only | identical to reference |
| EAGLE/MTP only | identical to reference |
| EAGLE/MTP + HiSparse | scheduler crash on the first request |
| mixed chunk only (concurrent requests) | ok |
| mixed chunk + HiSparse | scheduler crash on the first mixed batch |

## Modifications

Reject both at startup with a clear error, until HiSparse supports them (speculative decoding is in progress in #40670 / #37771, which can drop the check).

## Accuracy Tests

- With this change the speculative + HiSparse launch above exits at startup with `ValueError: --enable-hisparse does not support speculative decoding yet.`
- `test_server_args.py`, `test_model_overrides.py`: 385 passed.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- No new unit tests; this change only adds straightforward startup validation.

title: fix(frontend): reject out-of-range top_logprobs_num
body:
## Motivation

`top_logprobs_num` is a public logprob request parameter on the native `/generate` path. OpenAI `/v1/completions` `logprobs` and `/v1/chat/completions` `top_logprobs` are converted into the same internal field.

The tokenizer-side admission path validates `token_ids_logprob`, but it does not validate `top_logprobs_num`. The scheduler later calls `logprobs.topk(max_k, dim=-1)`, where the last dimension is the model vocab size. If one request asks for more top logprobs than the vocab contains, PyTorch raises `RuntimeError: selected index k out of range`; that scheduler exception triggers process-tree shutdown and makes the server unavailable for later requests.

I reproduced this on current main with a single native `/generate` request using `top_logprobs_num=100000` against a 32000-token vocab: the attack request disconnects, the server exits with `-9`, and both `/health_generate` and a normal `/generate` fail afterward.

## Modifications

- Add `_validate_top_logprobs_num` in `TokenizerManager`.
- Call it next to the existing `token_ids_logprob` validation for `GenerateReqInput`.
- Reject bool, non-integer, negative, and above-vocab values before the request reaches the scheduler.
- Keep `0 <= top_logprobs_num <= vocab_size` valid.
- Add focused unit coverage in the existing TokenizerManager unit test file.

## Testing

Real server before/after on A800-SXM4-80GB with `/root/autodl-tmp/models/tinyllama-w4a16-channel-v2`:

| Request | Current main | This patch |
|---|---|---|
| `/generate`, `top_logprobs_num=100000` | request disconnects, server exits `-9`, later requests fail | HTTP 400, health OK, later request OK |
| `/v1/completions`, `logprobs=100000` | same logprob path | HTTP 400, health OK, later request OK |
| `/v1/chat/completions`, `top_logprobs=100000` | same logprob path | HTTP 400, health OK, later request OK |

<details><summary>repro (server command, payloads, full output)</summary>

Environment:

- Hardware: NVIDIA A800-SXM4-80GB, CUDA SM80
- SGLang base: `3cb29f674`
- Model: `/root/autodl-tmp/models/tinyllama-w4a16-channel-v2`
- Vocab size: 32000
- Python: 3.12
- PyTorch: 2.11.0+cu130

Server:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /root/autodl-tmp/models/tinyllama-w4a16-channel-v2 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 31028 \
  --attention-backend triton \
  --sampling-backend pytorch \
  --disable-cuda-graph \
  --disable-piecewise-cuda-graph \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.5 \
  --dtype float16 \
  --max-running-requests 8
```

Native attack payload:

```json
{"text":"Hello","sampling_params":{"max_new_tokens":4,"temperature":0},"return_logprob":true,"top_logprobs_num":100000}
```

OpenAI completions attack payload:

```json
{"model":"/root/autodl-tmp/models/tinyllama-w4a16-channel-v2","prompt":"Hello","max_tokens":4,"temperature":0,"logprobs":100000}
```

OpenAI chat attack payload:

```json
{"model":"/root/autodl-tmp/models/tinyllama-w4a16-channel-v2","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":4,"logprobs":true,"top_logprobs":100000}
```

Current main, native `/generate`:

```text
MARKER_BASELINE_OK
MARKER_ATTACK_SENT gen_toplp
MARKER_ATTACK_RESULT gen_toplp status=None dt=5.1s body=RemoteDisconnected: Remote end closed connection without response
MARKER_HEALTH_AFTER gen_toplp fail:None
MARKER_NORMAL_AFTER gen_toplp fail:None body=URLError: <urlopen error [Errno 111] Connection refused>
MARKER_SERVER_EXIT gen_toplp -9
MARKER_DOS_CONFIRMED gen_toplp (server_exit=-9 health=None normal=None)
```

This patch, all three public entrypoints:

```text
MARKER_BASELINE_OK
MARKER_ATTACK_SENT gen_toplp
MARKER_ATTACK_RESULT gen_toplp status=400 dt=0.0s body={"error":{"message":"top_logprobs_num must be in [0, 32000], got 100000."}}

MARKER_NORMAL_AFTER gen_toplp ok
MARKER_SERVER_EXIT gen_toplp running
MARKER_ATTACK_SENT comp_logp
MARKER_ATTACK_RESULT comp_logp status=400 dt=0.0s body={"object":"error","message":"top_logprobs_num must be in [0, 32000], got 100000.","type":"BadRequestError","param":null,"code":400}
MARKER_HEALTH_AFTER comp_logp ok
MARKER_NORMAL_AFTER comp_logp ok
MARKER_SERVER_EXIT comp_logp running
MARKER_ATTACK_SENT chat_toplp
MARKER_ATTACK_RESULT chat_toplp status=400 dt=0.0s body={"object":"error","message":"top_logprobs_num must be in [0, 32000], got 100000.","type":"BadRequestError","param":null,"code":400}
MARKER_HEALTH_AFTER chat_toplp ok
MARKER_NORMAL_AFTER chat_toplp ok
MARKER_SERVER_EXIT chat_toplp running
```

</details>

Additional checks:

```bash
python -m pytest test/registered/unit/managers/test_tokenizer_manager_rid_cleanup.py -q
black --check python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py test/registered/unit/managers/test_tokenizer_manager_rid_cleanup.py

```
